column4: `<prefix>_search` is the search-loop entry of a generated artifact.
Signature: `int <prefix>_search(const unsigned char *s, size_t n, size_t startpos, ptrdiff_t (*caps)[2]);`
`<prefix>_search` searches `s[startpos..n)` for the leftmost match.
`<prefix>_search` returns `1` when a match is found.
On a match with `caps != NULL`, `<prefix>_search` writes `<PREFIX>_NCAPS` pairs to `caps`.
On a match, `caps[0]` is the whole-match span (there is no second name for it).
`<prefix>_search` returns `0` on no match.
On no match, `<prefix>_search` leaves `caps` (if non-NULL) untouched; the `int` return alone communicates match/no-match.
`<prefix>_search` returns `<PREFIX>_ERR_STEPS`, `<PREFIX>_ERR_FRAMES`, `<PREFIX>_ERR_WORK` or `<PREFIX>_ERR_RECURSE` when the engine gives up (see §4).
On an engine give-up return, `<prefix>_search` leaves `caps` untouched.
`<PREFIX>_ERR_RECURSE` is reserved and has no producer yet.
`PCREC_ERR_INTERNAL` is NOT a give-up (§4): it means the artifact detected its own analysis/emission inconsistency.
Today the only producer of `PCREC_ERR_INTERNAL` is module `lookaround`'s negative-polarity end-check.
On `PCREC_ERR_INTERNAL`, `caps` is left untouched like every other negative return.
`PCREC_ERR_STARTPOS` is NOT a give-up (§4): `startpos` is not a character boundary of the artifact's encoding, so the call is REFUSED and nothing is attempted.
On `PCREC_ERR_STARTPOS`, `caps` is left untouched.
Only an artifact compiled for an encoding with multi-byte characters can return `PCREC_ERR_STARTPOS`, and only when the startpos guard is not denied.
`PCREC_ERR_UTF` is NOT a give-up (§4): the artifact was compiled with `-futf-check` and an ill-formed sequence begins in the checked range `[startpos - LB, n)`.
On `PCREC_ERR_UTF` the call is refused before any attempt and `caps` is left untouched.
`<prefix>_valid_upto(s, n, startpos)` (§3.1.2) gives the offset of the ill-formed sequence behind `PCREC_ERR_UTF`.
Only a `-futf-check` artifact under an encoding with ill-formed byte strings can return `PCREC_ERR_UTF`.
A `0` return from `<prefix>_search` means no match, not a zero-length match.
A zero-length match in `<prefix>_search` is a success: it returns `1` with `caps[0][0] == caps[0][1]`.
The anchored entries (§3.2/§3.3) use the other convention: their return value carries a length, so `0` IS a zero-length match and no-match is `-1`.
Every return other than `1` leaves the whole `caps` array untouched, on every engine.
The leave-`caps`-untouched rule on non-`1` returns holds through every entry that takes `caps`: `_search`, `_search_in`, `_match_caps`, `_match_caps_in`.
The rule holds for an artifact whose groups above 0 can never be set (each reached only through a subroutine call or under `{0}`; a DFA artifact with `<PREFIX>_NCAPS >= 2`).
In such an artifact the unsettable group slots are written `PCREC_UNSET` on a success only, never on a no-match.
`tests/codegen/run_nomatch_caps.sh` checks the no-match-leaves-caps-untouched rule.
`caps` may be `NULL` for `<prefix>_search` (existence-only search).
`<prefix>_search` with `startpos > n` returns `0`.
In `<prefix>_search`, `^` anchors to absolute offset `0` regardless of `startpos`.
`s` may be `NULL` only when `n == 0`.
A search may begin its internal scan after `startpos` where a necessary literal proves no match begins earlier; its answer is the one a scan from `startpos` gives.
CHECK: The necessary-literal scan skip is reported through the `<PREFIX>_REQ_HANDOFF` stamp (§6.3).
The step budget meters only the work the matcher performs, so positions proven unable to begin a match consume none.
No artifact begins a scan later where that could change whether a budget-limited search answers or gives up (a count-collapsed prefilter declines).
`\G` keeps asserting at `startpos` itself even when the scan begins later.
A search may skip a START position whose byte cannot begin a match: a prefilter-less VM artifact attempts no match where the pattern's start set excludes the byte there.
CHECK: The start-set skip is reported through the `<PREFIX>_VM_START_SCAN` stamp (§6.3).
Positions that a start-set or necessary-literal proof excludes consume no budget and no capacity.

A search that gives up under `-fno-start-set` (on steps, work, backtrack frames, trail, or a caller-provided buffer's capacity in the `_in` entries) may return the answer an unbounded budget and capacity return.
A search under `-fno-start-set` never gives up where the default (with the skip) answers; an answer under `-fno-start-set` is the answer with the skip.
`startpos` MUST be a character boundary of the artifact's encoding, and by default the artifact enforces it.
Under the `byte` encoding every position is a character boundary and no startpos guard is emitted at all.
Under an encoding with multi-byte characters a `startpos` inside a character is refused with `PCREC_ERR_STARTPOS`.
`PCREC_ERR_STARTPOS` is a negative return below `PCREC_ERR_FLOOR` (§4) and not a give-up: nothing was attempted and no budget was spent.
The startpos-guard test is O(1) and reads at most one byte of `s`.

Under `PCRE2_UTF`, libpcre2 returns `PCRE2_ERROR_BADUTFOFFSET` for every mid-character `startoffset`; measured over ten patterns at both mid-character offsets of a two-character subject, 20 of 20 refused (libpcre2 10.46).
The same ten patterns answered normally at all three boundary offsets of the two-character subject (libpcre2 10.46; docs/design/utf8_measurements/out/startbnd.txt).
Under D26 pcrec owes the refusal of a mid-character startpos, not libpcre2's error number.
A `startpos` past the end of the subject returns `0` (the `startpos > n` check comes before the character-boundary guard).
Every position at or beyond `n` counts as a character boundary.
libpcre2 answers `PCRE2_ERROR_BADOFFSET` for a startoffset past the end; pcrec deliberately keeps returning `0` (a stated divergence).
The anchored entries (§3.2/§3.3) carry the same startpos guard against `ctx->pos`.
The `_in` entries of §10 inherit the startpos guard from the bodies they share.
`<prefix>_next_pos` (§3.1.1) is the supported way to produce a valid `startpos`.
The find-all loop uses `<prefix>_next_pos` on both arms, so the loop is unaffected by the startpos guard in either direction, ill-formed subjects included.
`-fno-startpos-guard` selects the other semantics: the artifact answers at whatever position the caller named, with the automaton's own answer.

Under `-fno-startpos-guard`, for a leading negative assertion the answer differs from both of PCRE2's UTF modes in the succeeding direction: `(?<!.)` at offset 1 of the bytes `CE B1 CE B2` reports `(1,1)`.
A truncated leading character has no path, and a negative assertion succeeds exactly where its body has none.
Neither the default guard arm nor `-fno-startpos-guard` rounds a caller's `startpos > 0`; neither silently advances to the next boundary.
`-fstartpos-guard=align` is the third value of the startpos-guard axis (`docs/spec/tuning.md` §2.23); it is rounding asked for by name.
`-fstartpos-guard=align` is for a caller holding a misaligned pointer into valid text.
Under `-fstartpos-guard=align`, a `startpos > 0` inside a character is moved FORWARD over continuation bytes to the next character start (or `n`), once, at entry.
Under `-fstartpos-guard=align` the search runs exactly as if the aligned position had been passed: `caps` offsets, `\G` and a lookbehind's context are all read from it.
Under `-fstartpos-guard=align`, offset 0 is never moved and never refused.
Under `-fstartpos-guard=align`, the anchored entries (§3.2/§3.3) answer `-1` at a misaligned `ctx->pos`, because no match begins inside a character.
`-fstartpos-guard=align` is refused together with `-fno-startpos-guard`.
`-fstartpos-guard=align` is inert under the `byte` encoding.
`-fstartpos-guard=align` is not a way to accept invalid UTF-8.

Under `-futf-check` with `-fstartpos-guard=align`, the check runs from the ALIGNED position, stepping back behind it as for any startpos, so the bytes of the character the pointer landed inside are checked as the caller's real text.
Offset 0 is never refused by the startpos guard.
On an ill-formed subject, offset 0 is not where a match is attempted if the subject begins with continuation bytes (`0x80`-`0xBF`): offset 0 is then not a character start.

When a subject begins with continuation bytes, the search begins at the first non-continuation byte (or at `n`), exactly as `PCRE2_MATCH_INVALID_UTF` advances its start offset, and every answer is the answer from there.
For a subject beginning with continuation bytes: `''`, `\B`, `x*` and `(?=)` report `(1,1)` on `\x80` and `(2,2)` on `\x80\x80`.
For a subject beginning with continuation bytes, `^`, `\A` and `\G` are FALSE at the moved start; `^` finds nothing on `\x80`.
`\G|b` reports `(2,3)` on `\x80\x80b` (libpcre2 10.46; docs/dev/lanes/k73utf_evidence/k73_witness_10.46.txt).
An ill-formed LEAD byte (`0xFF`, a truncated `0xE3`) is a valid start and is attempted.
The offset-0 start rule has NO FLAG: it is the same under `-fno-startpos-guard`, which governs only a `startpos > 0`.
The offset-0 start rule is the one place pcrec does what `PCRE2_MATCH_INVALID_UTF` does at a start offset.
An explicit mid-character `startpos > 0` keeps the `PCREC_ERR_STARTPOS` refusal: a deliberate, stated divergence from `PCRE2_MATCH_INVALID_UTF`.

The anchored entries (§3.2/§3.3) answer `-1` at `ctx->pos == 0` on a subject beginning with continuation bytes, because they report only a match beginning exactly at `ctx->pos` and none begins at a non-character-start.

libpcre2 under `PCRE2_ANCHORED` advances the start and reports the match at the moved start (`(1,1)` for `x*` on `\x80`); pcrec's anchored contract cannot report a start other than `ctx->pos`, a second stated divergence.
Both anchored entry shapes (§3.2/§3.3) agree on the `-1` answer at `ctx->pos == 0` on a continuation-leading subject.
An artifact compiled with `-futf-check` refuses an ill-formed subject with `PCREC_ERR_UTF`, as `PCRE2_UTF` does (axis: `docs/spec/tuning.md` §2.36).
By default an artifact is INVALID-TOLERANT: an ill-formed sequence matches nothing and nothing reports it (`PCRE2_MATCH_INVALID_UTF` semantics, K73's start rule).
A `-futf-check` artifact refuses the call with `PCREC_ERR_UTF` when an ill-formed sequence BEGINS anywhere in `[f, n)`, where `f` is `startpos` stepped back LB characters.
The `-futf-check` refusal happens before any attempt, whether or not a match lies before the bad bytes: `a` on `a\xff` is refused, as libpcre2 10.46 refuses it.
A `-futf-check` artifact otherwise answers exactly as the default artifact would.
LB is PCRE2's `max_lookbehind` fact: the widest lookbehind branch in characters, and 1 for `\b`, `\B` and `\A`.
LB is never summed through nesting, and dead code (a `(?(DEFINE)...)` body) counts.
`^`, `$`, `\G`, `\z`, `\Z` and `\K` count 0 toward LB.
Under `-futf-check`, `b` on `\xffab` from startpos 2 answers `(2,3)` while `(?<=..)b` there is refused.
The `-futf-check` step-back is PCRE2's raw walk: per character, one byte back and then back over every continuation byte, clamped at 0 and not validated.
Order of checks: the K50 startpos guard FIRST, then the `-futf-check` check (measured on libpcre2 10.46).
A mid-character `startpos > 0` is `PCREC_ERR_STARTPOS` whether or not the subject is well-formed.
Under `-fstartpos-guard=align` the `-futf-check` check runs from the aligned position.
`startpos > n` keeps returning `0` and is not checked by `-futf-check`.
At `startpos == 0` K50 does not refuse, so a subject that begins with a continuation byte is refused by the `-futf-check` check at offset 0.
Every entry that takes a subject performs the `-futf-check` check, at one site per body, beside the K50 guard.
The anchored entries (§3.2/§3.3) and §10's `_in` entries return `PCREC_ERR_UTF` on exactly the calls `<prefix>_search` refuses from the same position.
On the VM, a FRAMES escalation of the tiered default entry (§10.9) re-runs the body and validates a second time (the stated cost of re-running from scratch).
The `-futf-check` cost is one O(n) pass per call (directional: about as much again as a scanning call on sparse-accented text).
Under `-futf-check`, a call a prefilter would answer sublinearly becomes linear.
`-futf-check` is off by default because of its O(n) cost.
A find-all loop over a `-futf-check` artifact validates on every call; §3.1.2 gives the linear idiom.
Under the `byte` encoding `-futf-check` is inert: no check is emitted, `<PREFIX>_UTF_CHECK` reads `"inert"`, and the artifact is byte-identical to one built without the flag.
STATED DIVERGENCE: `PCRE2_UTF` clips backward reads at `f`; pcrec does not (measured on libpcre2 10.46 and 10.48).
Under `PCRE2_UTF`, libpcre2 treats `f` as the start of the subject for the backward reads a lookbehind or `\b` makes, even on well-formed text (libpcre2 10.46 and 10.48).
`(?<=\ba)b` on `"xab"` from startpos 2 reports `(2,3)` under `PCRE2_UTF`, though the same pattern finds nothing from 0 and finds nothing without UTF.
`(?<=(?<=..)a)b` on `"zzzab"` from startpos 4 finds nothing under `PCRE2_UTF` and reports `(4,5)` without it.
pcrec reads the real bytes with or without `-futf-check`: `(?<=\ba)b` on `"xab"` from 2 finds nothing and `(?<=(?<=..)a)b` on `"zzzab"` from 4 reports `(4,5)`.
pcrec's principle: a match's answer must not depend on where the caller started the search.
On the clip divergence, the refusal set and the refusal OFFSET are exact and unaffected; only the accepted ANSWER differs.
The clip divergence affects only patterns whose backward reach exceeds LB (three patterns in the pinned set).
The clip class is 4 cells per configuration, pinned EXACTLY (`CLIP` in `tests/utfcheck/check.py`, the `clip-*` populations).
A change in either engine moves a number rather than a sentence; a deliberate, stated divergence is the only allowed exception to D26's exactness of what a pattern matches.
What the artifact promises about its own positions is NOT part of the `-futf-check`/startpos-guard axis.

Every position the ENGINE generates (an unanchored search's candidate match starts, a failed attempt's retry, and the first attempt of a search at offset 0) is a character start of the encoding, unconditionally and under either setting of the startpos-guard flag.
A reported match span never begins inside a character on any subject, whichever startpos-guard arm the artifact carries.
The startpos-guard flag governs only where a CALLER may point the entry.
Every offset written to `caps` is an ABSOLUTE offset into `s`, never relative to `startpos`.
Measured: searching `"xabcabcx"` for `abc` from `startpos = 0` reports `[1,4)`, and the next search from `4` reports `[4,7)`, not `[0,3)`.
`caps[0][0]` is where REPORTING begins, which is not always where matching began.
`\K` resets the reported start to wherever the winning path last crossed it.
`a\Kb` over `"ab"` consumes two bytes from offset 0 and reports `[1,2)`.
`caps[0][0]` can be greater than the offset the match began at, so it is not a bound on where the engine looked.
The find-all loop advances off `caps[0][1]` (the match END), which `\K` does not touch.
`caps[0][0] == caps[0][1]` does not imply nothing was consumed under `\K`.
`ab\K` over `"ab"` reports `[2,2)` after consuming two bytes.
Under `\K`, the find-all loop stays correct: an empty REPORTED span at `p` advances by `<prefix>_next_pos` and the next search starts past it.
A caller that measures work done by the reported span width would measure zero under `\K` (`ab\K`).
The anchored entries of §3.2/§3.3 return the CONSUMED length, which is the number that differs from the reported span under `\K`.
On `ab\K` at `pos = 0` the anchored entries return `2` while the span they report (§3.3) is `[2,2)`.
Returning the consumed length from the anchored entries is deliberate and is what makes the §5 callout protocol's advance terminate.
A pattern with no `\K` is unaffected in every respect by the reporting-start rule.
The `\K` construct is module-gated (`assertions`) and, when present, forces the VM engine.
`<prefix>_search` on a DFA artifact has two forms, answer-identical and differing only in cost, reported by `<PREFIX>_DFA_START` (§6.3; tuning.md §2.19).
A DFA search normally runs two scans over the same bytes: a forward one to find where the match ends and a backward one over a second, independently built machine to find where it began.

On a pattern whose forward machine accepts before it reads a byte (`a*`, `.*`, `[a-z]{0,4096}` and that family), the compiler proves the second scan's answer is `startpos` and emits neither the scan nor the machine.
An artifact whose backward scan is proved away stamps `<PREFIX>_DFA_START "pinned"`; otherwise it stamps `"reverse-pass"`.
Nothing in the `<prefix>_search` contract changes between the pinned and reverse-pass forms.
Both forms report ABSOLUTE offsets into `s`; the pinned form writes `caps[0][0] = startpos`, never `0`.
Both forms keep the zero-length-match-is-a-success convention; the pinned form depends on it (the empty match at `startpos` is the answer it reports).
The only caller-observable differences between pinned and reverse-pass forms are cost (roughly a factor of two on a counted class run) and artifact size.
A pinned search still returns `0` on some calls.

A pinned search at `startpos > 0` on a machine whose start state depends on the byte before it (`\b`, `(?m)^`) can begin in a state from which nothing can match; no accept is recorded and `0` is the correct answer.
The emitted pinned artifact keeps the test that delivers that `0` and names it load-bearing so a coverage report does not mistake it for dead code.
`s` is `n` bytes and nothing more.
A `0x00` byte inside `s` is an ORDINARY byte with no special meaning; only the pattern side (§7) is NUL-terminated.
The matcher never reads `s[n]`: there is no sentinel, `s` need not be NUL-terminated and need not have a readable byte after its end.
Measured on both engines with the subject in an exact-size heap allocation under AddressSanitizer: `a.b` and `a(.)b` both match the 3 bytes `{'a', 0x00, 'b'}` (span `[0,3)`, group 1 `[1,2)`).
Matching, non-matching and `n == 0` searches over exact-size buffers are all ASan-clean on both engines.
The exact-size-buffer check is non-vacuous: the same probe compiled to read one byte past the end (`n` overstated by one) fires a heap-buffer-overflow at the matcher's own `memchr` prefilter.
`<prefix>_search` is ONE-SHOT: it finds the first match at or after `startpos`.
There is no batch find-all primitive and none is planned for v1; a caller wanting every match writes the loop.
The find-all loop is not simply "restart at the previous match's end", which spins forever the first time a pattern matches empty (`a*` on `"bbb"` returns `[0,0)` from `startpos = 0` for ever).

The find-all loop idiom: `p = 0; while (p <= n) { r = <prefix>_search(s,n,p,caps); if (r != 1) break; report(caps[0][0], caps[0][1]); p = (caps[0][1] > caps[0][0]) ? <prefix>_next_pos(s,n,(size_t)caps[0][1]-1) : <prefix>_next_pos(s,n,(size_t)caps[0][0]); }`.
In the find-all loop, `r == 0` means done and `r < 0` means the engine gave up (§4); both break the loop.
In the find-all loop, after a non-empty match the next position is `<prefix>_next_pos(s, n, caps[0][1] - 1)` (boundary-aligned resume at the match end).
In the find-all loop, after an EMPTY match the next position is `<prefix>_next_pos(s, n, caps[0][0])` (the next character after the match start).
The non-empty arm of the find-all loop is aligned, and the alignment is a no-op on a well-formed subject.
A non-empty match ends at a character boundary of a well-formed subject.
`<prefix>_next_pos(s, n, end - 1)` returns `end` itself under `byte` (where it is `end - 1 + 1`) and under `utf8`, on a well-formed subject.

The aligned non-empty arm differs from `p = end` only where the match ends immediately before a STRAY continuation byte (one that no lead byte claims): the loop steps over the stray to the next non-continuation byte.
The aligned non-empty arm avoids handing the engine a `startpos` the guard refuses (`PCREC_ERR_STARTPOS`) after a match ending before a stray continuation byte.
Measured: `a` over `a\x80a` under `-e utf8` with the unaligned loop reported 1 match, where libpcre2 with `PCRE2_MATCH_INVALID_UTF` driven through the same loop reports 2.
The subtraction `end - 1` in the loop cannot underflow because a non-empty match has `end >= 1`.
`end - 1 < n` keeps `<prefix>_next_pos` in its boundary-skipping domain (`pos >= n` is where it returns `pos + 1`).
A `startpos` the CALLER passes in must be a character boundary of the artifact's encoding.
A caller who names a continuation byte as `startpos` is REFUSED with `PCREC_ERR_STARTPOS`, whether the byte is inside a well-formed character or is a stray.

libpcre2 draws no line between a continuation byte inside a well-formed character and a stray: without `PCRE2_MATCH_INVALID_UTF` both are `PCRE2_ERROR_BADUTFOFFSET`, with it both are advanced (docs/dev/k75_measurement.md).
The positions the find-all loop computes are always boundaries: `0` (or the offset-0 rule's own start), a match end aligned as above, and the `<prefix>_next_pos` advance.
The find-all loop as written never triggers `PCREC_ERR_STARTPOS`, on a well-formed or an ill-formed subject.
A continuation byte is never a match START: every position the engine generates is a character start.
Stepping over a continuation byte, as the find-all loop does after a non-empty match and as `<prefix>_next_pos` does after an empty one, cannot lose a match.
The empty-match family at an ill-formed subject END is a separate matter (K74) and is not changed by the loop alignment.
Empty-match advance rule: a zero-length match is reported like any other, and then the next search starts at the next CHARACTER boundary past its start.
After a non-empty match the next search starts at the first boundary at or after its end (the aligned arm).
The empty-match advance is off the match's own START (`caps[0][0]`), not off the loop variable.
An empty match can be found at a position later than the one searched from.
The find-all loop terminates because `p` moves strictly forward every iteration and `p > n` ends it.
`<prefix>_next_pos` returns a position strictly greater than the one it was given (§3.1.1's contract).

The find-all loop was compiled against real artifacts and run against python3 `re.finditer` on twenty-six (pattern, subject) pairs, on both engines, each pattern compiled twice (captures-on and `--no-captures`), 52 runs.
The twenty-six pairs are `byte`-encoded; the ill-formed-subject witnesses are `tests/rxtsource/fixtures/mc_illformed_utf8.rxtin`.
Twenty-two of the twenty-six pairs agree with `re.finditer` span for span.
`a*` over `"bbb"` gives `(0,0) (1,1) (2,2) (3,3)` under the find-all loop, agreeing with `re.finditer`.
`x?y` over `"yy"` gives `(0,1) (1,2)` under the find-all loop, agreeing with `re.finditer`.
`a|` over `"bab"` gives `(0,0) (1,2) (2,2) (3,3)` under the find-all loop, agreeing with `re.finditer`.
`a|b*` over `"cbbac"` gives `(0,0) (1,3) (3,4) (4,4) (5,5)` under the find-all loop, agreeing with `re.finditer`.
The find-all loop also agrees with `re.finditer` on `a*`/`"aaa"`, `a?`/`"aba"`, `b*`/`"abbbab"`, `(a|)`/`"xax"`, `a(b|)c`/`"acabc"`, `(ab)*`/`"ababx"`, `a{0,2}`/`"aaaa"`, `[a-c]*`/`"xabcx"`.

The find-all loop also agrees on `[0-9]+`/`"a12b345"`, `a{2,}`/`"aaaa"`, `(?:ab|a)`/`"aab"`, `(a*)*`/`"aab"`, `.`/`"abc"`, `ab$`/`"xabab"`, `^a`/`"aa"`, `c*` and `x` over the EMPTY subject, and `a`/`"a"`.
The whole find-all measurement set is `tests/encseam/findall_cases.txt` and it runs in `make test`.
The find-all loop is LOSSY: it reports fewer matches than PCRE2 and python `re` for a pattern that prefers the empty match at a position where a non-empty match also starts.
PCRE2 and python `re`, on finding an empty match at `p`, retry at `p` with "empty match not permitted here" (`PCRE2_NOTEMPTY_ATSTART`) and report the non-empty match too, before moving on.
pcrec's entry points cannot express the NOTEMPTY_ATSTART retry: no entry has a "must not match empty here" mode, so the advance rule is the whole of what a pcrec consumer can do.
All measured divergences of the find-all loop are OMISSIONS: the loop's spans are always a strict SUBSET of `re.finditer`'s, which the suite checks.
`|a` over `"aaa"`: the find-all loop reports 4 spans `(0,0) (1,1) (2,2) (3,3)` where `re.finditer` reports 7, adding `(0,1) (1,2) (2,3)`.
`a*?` over `"aaa"`: the find-all loop reports 4 spans vs 7 for `re.finditer`.
`a??` over `"aba"`: the find-all loop reports 4 spans vs 6 for `re.finditer`.
`b*?` over `"abba"`: the find-all loop reports 5 spans vs 7 for `re.finditer`.
Where the pattern's own preference picks a non-empty match wherever one starts (every greedy quantifier among the agreeing cases), the find-all loop has no divergence.
The find-all loop is what gives `\G` its meaning.
`\G` asserts that the current position equals the `startpos` the call was given.
Under the find-all loop (which passes its resume position as `startpos`), `\G` means "contiguous with the previous match", which is PCRE2's global-iteration semantics.
`\G\w+` under the find-all loop is a TOKENIZER: it reports `(0,2)` on `"ab ab ab"` and stops at the first gap, where the `\G`-free `\w+` reports all three.
Measured by `tests/assertions/run_gstart_diff.sh` §1 against libpcre2 driven through the same loop (not a hand-written span list).
`\K` under the find-all loop is safe: the loop advances off `caps[0][1]` and `\K` moves only `caps[0][0]`, so termination and progress are untouched.
A `\K` pattern can report an empty span after consuming bytes (`ab\K` gives `[2,2)`), which takes the loop's EMPTY arm and advances one character from the REPORTED START rather than the match end.
`ab\K` over `"ababab"` reports `2,2 6,6` under the find-all loop, from both pcrec and libpcre2 driven through the same loop.
Under the find-all loop's empty arm the match at offset 2..4 of `ab\K` over `"ababab"` is not reported again at 4.
`a\Kb` over `"ababab"` reports `1,2 3,4 5,6` under the find-all loop, from both pcrec and libpcre2.
`tests/assertions/run_kreset_diff.sh` §5 is the `\K` find-all comparison against libpcre2 and runs every suite.
The loop's empty arm is written against `caps[0][0]` rather than the loop variable because an empty match can be found at a different offset from the one asked for, which `\K` makes routine.
In the shipped DFA emitter (`src/gen/emit_dfa.c`), the DFA matcher writes `caps[0][0]`/`caps[0][1]` only under `if (caps)` in the unanchored search body.

Every artifact carries `<prefix>_next_pos` as a fifth exported entry.
The find-all loop's advance goes through `<prefix>_next_pos`, not `+ 1`.
Signature: `size_t <prefix>_next_pos(const unsigned char *s, size_t n, size_t pos);`
`<prefix>_next_pos` is the one place an artifact's byte-vs-character distinction lives.
An artifact embeds exactly one encoding's residual block, chosen per compile call by `pcrec_options.encoding` (§8.2), never process- or file-globally.
Two differently-prefixed artifacts compiled for different encodings compose in one translation unit.
`<prefix>_next_pos` returns the smallest position STRICTLY GREATER than `pos` that is a character boundary of the artifact's encoding, counting every position >= `n` as a boundary.
The result of `<prefix>_next_pos` is in `(pos, n]` whenever `pos < n`.
The result of `<prefix>_next_pos` is `pos + 1` whenever `pos >= n`; this is what lets a find-all loop advance past a zero-length match and still terminate.
`<prefix>_next_pos` reads `s` only at offsets in `[pos, n)`, so the `(s == NULL, n == 0)` subject that `<prefix>_search` accepts is legal there too.
`<prefix>_next_pos` is never called from the artifact's own engine; it is caller-facing residue, not hot-path code.
An artifact compiled for a different encoding exports the same `<prefix>_next_pos` entry with that encoding's body, and no caller loop changes.
`<prefix>_next_pos` is an ordinary extern function, not a macro and not `static inline`.
`<prefix>_next_pos` is declared in the emitted header (or, in a self-contained artifact, in the `.c` beside the other entries' declarations) and defined in the `.c`.
`<prefix>_next_pos` never reads outside `[pos, n)`.
Under the byte encoding `<prefix>_next_pos` does not read `s` at all.
`pos > n` is not an error for `<prefix>_next_pos`: the result is simply `pos + 1`.
The result of `<prefix>_next_pos` is always strictly greater than `pos`.
Under the byte encoding the body of `<prefix>_next_pos` is `return pos + 1;` (with `s` and `n` unused).
Under `utf8` the advance of `<prefix>_next_pos` is defined on every input, well-formed or not, and the rule is normative.
Under `utf8`, `<prefix>_next_pos` advances from `pos + 1` past every byte in the range `0x80`-`0xBF`, stopping at the first byte outside that range or at `n`.
Under `utf8`, a well-formed character is skipped whole by `<prefix>_next_pos`.
Under `utf8`, a truncated or otherwise ill-formed sequence degrades under `<prefix>_next_pos` to the next non-continuation byte, not a position in the middle of the garbage.
The four `<prefix>_next_pos` promises (extern, bounded reads, `pos > n` ok, strictly greater) hold unchanged under `utf8` on ill-formed input.
The `utf8` `<prefix>_next_pos` loop is bounded by `n`, not by a well-formed character's maximum of three continuation bytes, which makes the degradation total.
The `utf8` body of `<prefix>_next_pos` is: `size_t i = pos + 1; while (i < n && (s[i] & 0xC0) == 0x80) i++; return i;`.
The `utf8` `<prefix>_next_pos` rule is the entry's own rule, the encoding seam's, and K49's retry advance.
`docs/spec/rxt_format.md`'s `mc` production is the consumer that reads the `utf8` `<prefix>_next_pos` rule and states the same rule.
The find-all loop is final: M5's UTF-8 backend supplies a boundary-aware `<prefix>_next_pos` under the same signature and no caller's find-all loop changes.
A consumer must NOT inline `+ 1` in place of `<prefix>_next_pos`: that makes a byte-compiled caller wrong against a UTF-8-compiled artifact.
CHECK: `<prefix>_next_pos` under `utf8` skips forward over continuation bytes to the next character boundary, and the find-all loop compiles unchanged against a `-e utf8` artifact.
The encoding constant is `PCREC_ENC_BYTE` and the CLI encoding value is `byte` (the semantics are "every byte is a character"); there is no `PCREC_ENC_ASCII` (§8.2 records the rename).
A residual entry is never called from the artifact's own engine (DD-12 (7) forbids the hot path depending on the encoding).
`tests/codegen/run_codegen_tests.sh` reads every emitted engine body for a residual reference across six emission shapes in both artifact forms.
The residual-in-engine check is sabotage-validated by `tests/mech/sabotages/S68_residual_in_hot_loop.sh` (the emitted bitmap prefilter's skip loop advancing through `<prefix>_next_pos`).
Under the byte backend the sabotaged advance and `+ 1` are the same value, so the whole `.rxt` corpus stays green and only the structural check sees the sabotage.
`<prefix>_valid_upto` is the subject validator (UTF-VALID).
Signature: `size_t <prefix>_valid_upto(const unsigned char *s, size_t n, size_t startpos);`

`<prefix>_valid_upto` returns the offset of the FIRST BYTE of the first ill-formed sequence of the artifact's encoding that begins at or after `f`, where `f` is `startpos` stepped back LB characters by PCRE2's raw walk.
`<prefix>_valid_upto` returns `n` when there is no ill-formed sequence, and `n` when `startpos > n`.
The offset `<prefix>_valid_upto` returns is the sequence's lead byte, or a stray continuation byte itself.

That offset equals `PCRE2_UTF`'s own error offset (`pcre2_get_startchar`) on every measured kind: truncated, overlong, surrogate, above U+10FFFF, `0xF5`-`0xFF`, isolated continuation (libpcre2 10.46; docs/design/utf_valid_design.md §1).
EVERY artifact exports `<prefix>_valid_upto`, whatever `-futf-check` says.
Under `byte`, the body of `<prefix>_valid_upto` is `return n;` and `s` is never read, so the `(s == NULL, n == 0)` subject is legal there too.
A caller's code using `<prefix>_valid_upto` compiles unchanged across encodings.
A `-futf-check` artifact refuses exactly the calls for which `<prefix>_valid_upto` returns `< n`.
The value `<prefix>_valid_upto` returns is the offset of the `-futf-check` refusal when passed the SAME `startpos` the refused call was given (under `-fstartpos-guard=align`, the aligned one).
The step-back happens INSIDE `<prefix>_valid_upto`, so a lookbehind-window error before `startpos` is reported, not missed.
`<prefix>_valid_upto` is called once per call from the entry, never from an engine body.
The [M5-SEAM] structural check counts the call sites of `<prefix>_valid_upto` like those of `<prefix>_next_pos`.
LB reaches the `<prefix>_valid_upto` body as `<prefix>_VALID_LB`, a `.c`-only macro, and is otherwise not part of the contract.
`<prefix>_valid_upto` does not refuse a mid-character `startpos`: with LB 0 the walk starts ON the continuation byte, which is then reported as ill-formed.
The checking entries never ask the mid-character question of `<prefix>_valid_upto`, because the K50 guard (or the alignment) runs first.
Find-all over a `-futf-check` artifact validates `[f, n)` on every call, so `m` matches cost O(n*m) validation bytes (PCRE2's own property, for which it documents `PCRE2_NO_UTF_CHECK`).
The linear idiom for find-all under the check needs ONE artifact compiled WITHOUT `-futf-check`.
Linear idiom: if `<prefix>_valid_upto(s, n, 0) != n` refuse (the offset is the return); otherwise run the §3.1 find-all loop unchanged on the same default artifact.
The default artifact in the validate-once idiom answers exactly as the checking artifact would on every call of the loop, because every call's checked range lies inside `[0, n)`.
A validity cursor kept inside the artifact across calls is not offered, because §5.3's reentrancy contract forbids the state.
The per-call "check as you move forward" contract (`-futf-check=extent`) is RESERVED and refused until a caller measures a need for it.
